notes.front: What is Compute Engine?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s infrastructure-as-a-service product, offering self-managed virtual machine instances and bare metal instances.
notes.explanation: It offers virtual machines on a hypervisor, with Linux and Windows operating systems and durable storage options.
notes.example: Like renting a server in a data centre, but you create it in minutes and pay only for the resources you use.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compute Engine overview”, “Compute Engine overview”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine is an infrastructure as a service (IaaS) product that offers self-managed virtual machine (VM) instances and bare metal instances. Compute Engine offers VMs with a KVM hypervisor, operating systems for both Linux and Windows, and durable storage options.

notes.front: What is a machine family in Compute Engine?
notes.back: A curated set of processor and hardware configurations optimised for specific workloads, such as general-purpose or memory-optimised.
notes.explanation: Families are divided further into machine series, such as the low-cost E series, and you then choose a machine type within a series.
notes.example: Like deciding between a van, a sports car and a minibus before choosing the exact model.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Compute Engine terminology”
notes.evidence: Machine family: A curated set of processor and hardware configurations optimized for specific workloads, for example, General-purpose, Accelerator-optimized, or Memory-optimized.

notes.front: What is a predefined machine type?
notes.back: A machine type with a preset number of vCPUs and amount of memory, charged at a set price.
notes.explanation: Compute Engine offers these ready-made shapes when you create a virtual machine; if none meets your needs, you can set the hardware yourself.
notes.example: Like buying a laptop in one of the shop’s fixed configurations instead of choosing each component.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine offers predefined machine types that you can use when you create a VM instance. A predefined machine type has a preset number of vCPUs and amount of memory, and is charged at a set price. If predefined VMs don't meet your needs, you can create a VM instance with custom virtualized hardware settings.

notes.front: What is a custom machine type?
notes.back: A virtual machine shape with a number of vCPUs and an amount of memory that you choose, instead of a preset shape.
notes.explanation: Instead of accepting a predefined shape, you set the vCPU count and the memory directly.
notes.example: Like a made-to-measure suit instead of a standard size off the rail.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”
notes.evidence: Specifically, you can create a VM instance with a custom number of vCPUs and amount of memory, effectively using a custom machine type.

notes.front: What is a shared-core machine type?
notes.back: A machine type that timeshares a physical core: a cost-effective way to run small, non-resource-intensive apps.
notes.explanation: Several VMs take turns on one physical core, which keeps the cost low for apps that need little processing.
notes.example: Like a hot desk shared by several part-time staff instead of a private office each.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Shared-core machine types”
notes.evidence: These machine types timeshare a physical core which can be a cost-effective method for running small, non-resource-intensive apps.

notes.front: What is a Spot VM?
notes.back: A VM that uses excess Compute Engine capacity at a large discount, but which Compute Engine can preempt at any time.
notes.explanation: To preempt is to stop or delete the VM to reclaim the capacity; Spot VMs are the latest version of preemptible VMs.
notes.example: Like a standby airline seat: far cheaper, but you can be taken off when the airline needs the seat.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Spot VMs”
notes.evidence: This page describes Spot VMs: virtual machine (VM) instances that are excess Compute Engine capacity. Spot VMs have significant discounts, but Compute Engine might preemptively stop or delete (preempt) Spot VMs to reclaim the capacity at any time. Spot VMs are the latest version of preemptible VMs.

notes.front: What is an instance template?
notes.back: A saved set of VM configuration details from which you create Compute Engine instances.
notes.explanation: One template can launch as many instances as you need, each configured exactly the way you want.
notes.example: Like a recipe card: every cake baked from it comes out the same.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Disaster recovery building blocks”, “Instance templates”
notes.evidence: You can use Compute Engine instance templates to save the configuration details of the VM and then create Compute Engine instances from existing instance templates. You can use the template to launch as many instances as you need, configured exactly the way you want

notes.front: What is a managed instance group (MIG)?
notes.back: A group that runs an app on multiple identical VMs, with automated services such as autoscaling, autohealing and automatic updating.
notes.explanation: Those automated services are how a MIG makes a workload scalable and highly available.
notes.example: Like a depot running a fleet of identical delivery vans: it replaces broken vans and adds more at busy times.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Instance groups”
notes.evidence: Managed instance groups (MIGs) let you operate apps on multiple identical VMs. You can make your workloads scalable and highly available by taking advantage of automated MIG services, including: autoscaling, autohealing, regional (multiple zone) deployment, and automatic updating.

notes.front: What is autohealing in a MIG?
notes.back: The MIG automatically recreating a VM when a health check finds that the application on it has failed.
notes.explanation: The health-check signal picks up application-specific issues such as freezing, crashing or overloading.
notes.example: Like a shop manager who swaps out a till as soon as it freezes, instead of waiting for it to be unplugged.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Autohealing”
notes.evidence: Application-based autohealing improves application availability by relying on a health checking signal that detects application-specific issues such as freezing, crashing, or overloading. If a health check determines that an application has failed on a VM, the group automatically recreates that VM instance.

notes.front: What is a stateful managed instance group?
notes.back: A MIG that preserves each instance’s unique state (instance name, attached disks and metadata) across restarts, recreation, autohealing and updates.
notes.explanation: Keeping that state is what lets MIGs run stateful applications such as databases, legacy monoliths or long batch computations with checkpointing.
notes.example: Like hotel rooms that are cleaned and repaired between visits but keep the same guest’s luggage in place.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: You can use MIGs for building highly available deployments and automating operation of applications with stateful data or configuration, such as databases, DNS servers, legacy monolith applications, or long-running batch computations with checkpointing. Stateful MIGs preserve each instance's unique state (instance name, attached persistent disks, and metadata) on machine restart, recreation, auto-healing, and update events.

notes.front: What does the autoscaler do for a MIG?
notes.back: It adds or deletes VMs in the MIG automatically, based on the measured load and the autoscaling policy you define.
notes.explanation: Adding VMs when load rises is scaling out; deleting them when fewer are needed is scaling in.
notes.example: Like a supermarket opening more tills as the queues grow and closing them when it goes quiet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Autoscaling groups of instances”
notes.evidence: You define the autoscaling policy and the autoscaler performs automatic scaling based on the measured load and the options you configure. Autoscaling works by adding more VMs to your MIG when there is more load (scaling out), and deleting VMs when the need for VMs is lowered (scaling in).

notes.front: What is predictive autoscaling?
notes.back: An autoscaler mode that forecasts load from historical data and scales a MIG out before the predicted load arrives.
notes.explanation: Scaling out in advance means the new instances are ready to serve when the load comes.
notes.example: Like a bakery that bakes extra loaves before the Saturday rush because past Saturdays were busy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Predictive autoscaling”
notes.evidence: If you enable predictive autoscaling to optimize your MIG for availability, the autoscaler forecasts future load based on historical data and scales out a MIG in advance of predicted load, so that new instances are ready to serve when the load arrives.

notes.front: What is schedule-based autoscaling?
notes.back: Autoscaling that allocates capacity for anticipated loads: a minimum number of VMs for a set start time, duration and recurrence.
notes.explanation: Each schedule states the capacity and when it applies; a group can have up to 128 schedules.
notes.example: Like rostering extra staff every weekday at 9 a.m. because you know that is when the doors open.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Schedules”
notes.evidence: You can use schedule-based autoscaling to allocate capacity for anticipated loads. You can have up to 128 scaling schedules per instance group. For each scaling schedule, specify the following: Capacity: minimum required VM instances Schedule: start time, duration, and recurrence (for example, once, daily, weekly, or monthly)

notes.front: What is the autoscaler’s initialization period?
notes.back: The time applications take to initialise on new VM instances; it was formerly called the cool-down period.
notes.explanation: While an app is starting, the VM’s usage data might not reflect normal circumstances, so the autoscaler uses this period in its scaling decisions.
notes.example: Like a new employee’s first week, when their output does not yet show what they can do.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Initialization period”
notes.evidence: The initialization period, formerly known as cool down period, is the duration it takes for applications to initialize on your VM instances. While an application is initializing on an instance, the instance's usage data might not reflect normal circumstances. So the autoscaler uses the initialization period for scaling decisions

notes.front: What is a sole-tenant node?
notes.back: A physical Compute Engine server dedicated to hosting only your project’s VMs.
notes.explanation: It keeps your VMs physically separate from other projects’ VMs, or groups your VMs together on the same host hardware.
notes.example: Like renting a whole house instead of a flat in a shared block.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sole-tenancy overview”, “Sole-tenancy overview”
notes.evidence: Sole-tenancy provides exclusive access to a sole-tenant node, a physical Compute Engine server that is dedicated to hosting only your project's VMs. Use sole-tenant nodes to keep your VMs physically separated from VMs in other projects, or to group your VMs together on the same host hardware

notes.front: What does VM Manager’s Patch feature do?
notes.back: It applies operating system patches across a set of Compute Engine VMs.
notes.explanation: Long-running VMs need periodic system updates to protect them against defects and vulnerabilities.
notes.example: Like a building manager who services every flat’s boiler on a timetable, instead of each tenant arranging their own.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About Patch”, “About Patch”
notes.evidence: Note: This page describes the Patch feature in VM Manager and how it works. To create patch jobs, see Creating patch jobs. Use Patch to apply operating system patches across a set of Compute Engine VM instances (VMs). Long running VMs require periodic system updates to protect against defects and vulnerabilities.

notes.front: What is Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s managed implementation of Kubernetes, the open-source container orchestration platform.
notes.explanation: With it you deploy and operate your own containerised applications at scale on Google Cloud’s infrastructure.
notes.example: Like hiring a port authority to run the cranes and berths while you decide which containers go where.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “GKE overview”
notes.evidence: GKE is a managed implementation of the Kubernetes open source container orchestration platform. Kubernetes was developed by Google, drawing on years of experience operating production workloads at scale on Borg, Google's in-house cluster management system. With GKE, you can deploy and operate your own containerized applications at scale using Google Cloud's infrastructure.

notes.front: What is Autopilot in GKE?
notes.back: A GKE mode of operation in which Google manages your infrastructure configuration, including nodes, scaling and security.
notes.explanation: It provisions compute resources from your Kubernetes manifests and is optimised to run most production workloads.
notes.example: Like a fully serviced office: you bring the team, and the landlord handles desks, heating and repairs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE Autopilot overview”, “What is Autopilot?”
notes.evidence: GKE Autopilot is a mode of operation in GKE in which Google manages your infrastructure configuration, including your nodes, scaling, security, and other preconfigured settings. Autopilot mode is optimized to run most production workloads, and provisions compute resources based on your Kubernetes manifests.

notes.front: What is Cloud Run?
notes.back: A fully managed application platform that runs your code, function or container on Google’s highly scalable infrastructure.
notes.explanation: You supply code, a function or a container, and the platform runs it for you.
notes.example: Like a taxi for code: you say where to go, and you never own or service the car.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “What is Cloud Run”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run is a fully managed application platform for running your code, function, or container on top of Google's highly scalable infrastructure.

notes.front: What is scale to zero on Cloud Run?
notes.back: Cloud Run removing even the last remaining instance of a service when no requests are coming in.
notes.explanation: An idle service then runs no instances at all until the next request arrives.
notes.example: Like corridor lights on a motion sensor that switch off completely when nobody is there.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Scale to zero”
notes.evidence: If there are no incoming requests to your service, even the last remaining instance will be removed. This behavior is commonly referred to as scale to zero.

notes.front: What are Cloud Run functions?
notes.back: The latest version of functions on Google Cloud: each function is deployed as a service on Cloud Run.
notes.explanation: A function is not a separate kind of platform here: it runs as a Cloud Run service.
notes.example: Like a small kiosk inside a shopping centre: it does one job but uses the centre’s doors, power and security.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compare Cloud Run functions”, “Comparison”
notes.evidence: There are two versions of Cloud Run functions: Cloud Run functions, is the latest version of functions, deployed as a service on Cloud Run.

notes.front: What is Google Cloud VMware Engine?
notes.back: A fully managed service that lets you run the VMware platform in Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: It keeps operational continuity with existing VMware environments while integrating with Google Cloud services.
notes.example: Like moving your office to a new building with the same furniture and filing system, so nobody has to relearn where things are.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud VMware Engine is a fully managed service that lets you run the VMware platform in Google Cloud. This service helps you to retain operational continuity with your existing VMware environments, and enables seamless integration with Google Cloud services.

notes.front: Which Compute Engine machine family offers the best price-performance ratio for a variety of workloads?
notes.back: General-purpose.
notes.explanation: Its focus is balance across many kinds of workload, not the most of any one resource.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: General-purpose—best price-performance ratio for a variety of workloads.

notes.front: Which machine family suits workloads that are low in core usage and high in storage density?
notes.back: Storage-optimized.
notes.explanation: It pairs relatively few cores with a lot of storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Storage-optimized—best for workloads that are low in core usage and high in storage density.

notes.front: Which machine family is designed for high performance computing and compute-intensive workloads, with high performance per core?
notes.back: Compute-optimized.
notes.explanation: Its distinguishing claim is high performance per core.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Compute-optimized—designed for high performance computing (HPC) solutions and compute-intensive workloads; offers high performance per core on Compute Engine.

notes.front: Which machine family is purpose-built for input/output-intensive workloads that need high network bandwidth and packet processing performance?
notes.back: Network-optimized.
notes.explanation: It also offers superior block storage throughput per vCPU, which suits input/output-heavy work.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Network-optimized—purpose-built for IO-intensive workloads that require high network bandwidth, superior packet processing performance, and superior block storage throughput and IOPS per vCPU.

notes.front: Which machine family offers more memory per core than the other families, with up to 12 terabytes of memory?
notes.back: Memory-optimized.
notes.explanation: It is aimed at memory-intensive workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Memory-optimized—ideal for memory-intensive workloads, offering more memory per core than other machine families, with up to 12 TB of memory.

notes.front: Which machine family is the best option for workloads that need accelerators such as GPUs or TPUs?
notes.back: Accelerator-optimized.
notes.explanation: It targets massively parallel workloads such as machine learning and high performance computing.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Accelerator-optimized—ideal for massively parallelized Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) compute workloads, such as machine learning (ML) and high performance computing (HPC). This family is the best option for workloads that require accelerators (GPUs or TPUs).

notes.front: In a predefined machine type name such as n2-standard-4, what memory-to-vCPU ratio does “standard” mean?
notes.back: From 3 to 7 gigabytes of memory per vCPU, typically 4.
notes.explanation: The ratio names differ: highcpu types, for example, have from 1 to 3 gigabytes per vCPU.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Predefined machine types”
notes.evidence: Predefined machine types use a variety of vCPU to memory ratios: highcpu — from 1 to 3 GB memory per vCPU; typically, 2 GB memory per vCPU. standard — from 3 to 7 GB memory per vCPU; typically, 4 GB memory per vCPU.

notes.front: Which machine series can use custom machine types?
notes.back: The general-purpose family’s N and E series only, plus one accelerator-optimized series.
notes.explanation: Custom shapes are not available across every family, so the choice of family can rule them out.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”
notes.evidence: Custom machine types are available for the following: General-purpose machine family for the N and E machine series only. You can create a custom VM on the N4, N4D, N4A, N2, N2D, E2, or N1 machine series. Accelerator-optimized machine family for the G2 machine series only.

notes.front: On-demand prices for custom machine types include a {{c1::5%}} premium over the on-demand prices for predefined machine types.
notes.explanation: Custom VMs are charged by the vCPUs and memory hours they use, which differs from how predefined types are charged.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Custom machine type pricing”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud charges for custom VMs based on the number of vCPUs and memory hours that the VM uses. This is different from how predefined machine types are charged. The on-demand prices for custom machine types include a 5% premium over the on-demand prices for predefined machine types.

notes.front: What is extended memory on a custom machine type?
notes.back: Memory per vCPU beyond the series’ default maximum, up to the series limit, bought at a premium.
notes.explanation: For some workloads the default maximum memory per vCPU might not be enough.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Extended memory”
notes.evidence: Each custom machine type machine series has a default RAM maximum per vCPU. For some workloads, this might not be enough memory per vCPU. For a premium, you can get more memory per vCPU beyond the default maximum up to the machine series limit. This is referred to as extended memory.

notes.front: Spot VMs can cost up to {{c1::91%}} less than the on-demand price of standard VMs.
notes.explanation: The discount comes with a catch: Compute Engine might preempt them at any time, for example when it needs the resources for other tasks.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs are available at much lower prices—up to 91% discounts for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs, and Local SSDs—compared to the on-demand price for standard VMs. However, Compute Engine might preempt Spot VMs at any time, such as when it needs the resources for other tasks.

notes.front: Do Spot VMs have a minimum or maximum runtime?
notes.back: No, unless you specifically limit the runtime.
notes.explanation: Runtime is open-ended by default; any limit is one you choose. Preemption can still come at any time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs don't have a minimum or maximum runtime unless you specifically limit the runtime.

notes.front: Are Spot VMs covered by the Compute Engine Service Level Agreement?
notes.back: No. They are excluded from the Compute Engine Service Level Agreement and are not covered by any other.
notes.explanation: The stated reason is their limitations: they cannot live migrate to become standard VMs or restart automatically after a host event.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Spot VMs limitations”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs can't live migrate to become standard VMs while they are running or be set to automatically restart when there is a host event. Due to the preceding limitations, Spot VMs are not covered by any Service Level Agreement and are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA.

notes.front: How can a workload on a Spot VM detect that it is being preempted?
notes.back: By monitoring the preempted value in the VM’s default metadata, which Compute Engine sets to true.
notes.explanation: Updating that metadata value is how Compute Engine sends the preemption notice.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Preemption process”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine sends a preemption notice to the VM by updating the preempted value in your VM's default metadata to TRUE, which your workload can monitor to detect preemption.

notes.front: Why can you recreate a VM anywhere in Google Cloud from an existing instance template?
notes.back: Instance templates are globally replicated.
notes.explanation: That makes a template a disaster-recovery building block: the same configuration is available wherever you need to rebuild.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Disaster recovery building blocks”, “Instance templates”
notes.evidence: Instance templates are globally replicated, so you can recreate the instance anywhere in Google Cloud with the same configuration.

notes.front: Compute Engine maintains each of a MIG’s managed instances based on the configuration in an {{c1::instance template}}.
notes.explanation: An optional stateful configuration can sit alongside the template.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Managed instance groups (MIGs)”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine maintains each of the MIG's managed instances based on the configuration that you specify in an instance template and optional stateful configuration.

notes.front: What does a MIG do when one of its VMs crashes, is preempted or is deleted by an action the MIG did not start?
notes.back: It automatically recreates the VM from its original configuration: same VM name, same template.
notes.explanation: The recreated VM can then resume its work.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: If a VM in the group stops, crashes, gets preempted (Spot VMs), or is deleted by an action not initiated by the MIG, the MIG automatically recreates that VM based on its original configuration (same VM name, same template) so that the VM can resume its work.

notes.front: What is the difference between a zonal MIG and a regional MIG?
notes.back: A zonal MIG deploys instances to a single zone; a regional MIG deploys them across multiple zones in the same region.
notes.explanation: Spreading load across zones protects the workload against a zonal failure.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Regional or zonal groups”
notes.evidence: A zonal MIG, which deploys instances to a single zone. A regional MIG, which deploys instances to multiple zones across the same region. Both types offer all of the advantages of MIGs. Regional MIGs add higher availability by spreading application load across multiple zones, which protects your workload against zonal failure

notes.front: When rolling out an update to a MIG, what does a partial rollout allow?
notes.back: Canary testing: the new version goes to only part of the group first.
notes.explanation: You control the speed and scope of an update rollout to minimise disruption to the application.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Automatic updating”
notes.evidence: You can control the speed and scope of the update rollout in order to minimize disruptions to your application. You can optionally perform partial rollouts, which allows for canary testing.

notes.front: What does a MIG health check cause that a load-balancing health check does not?
notes.back: Deletion and recreation of instances that become unhealthy; load-balancing checks only steer traffic away.
notes.explanation: The same kind of check has a different consequence depending on what uses it; Google advises separate checks for the two in most scenarios.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Health checking”
notes.evidence: Load balancing health checks help direct traffic away from non-responsive instances and toward healthy instances; these health checks do not cause Compute Engine to recreate instances. On the other hand, managed instance group health checks proactively signal to delete and recreate instances that become UNHEALTHY. For the majority of scenarios, use separate health checks for load balancing and for autohealing.

notes.front: When an autoscaling policy has several signals, how does the autoscaler set the group’s recommended size?
notes.back: It calculates a recommended number of VMs for each signal and uses the largest.
notes.explanation: Taking the largest means every signal gets at least the capacity it calls for.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Autoscaling policy”
notes.evidence: When you set multiple signals in a policy, the autoscaler calculates the recommended number of VMs for each signal and sets your group's recommended size to the largest number.

notes.front: What three kinds of target utilisation metric can a MIG autoscale on?
notes.back: Average CPU utilisation, HTTP load-balancing serving capacity and Cloud Monitoring metrics.
notes.explanation: Each reflects the load of the instance group, and a policy can use one or more of them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Target utilization metrics”
notes.evidence: You can autoscale based on one or more of the following metrics that reflect the load of the instance group: Average CPU utilization HTTP load balancing serving capacity Cloud Monitoring metrics

notes.front: Can a MIG that autoscales on average CPU utilisation scale in to zero instances?
notes.back: No. CPU utilisation, load-balancing serving capacity and per-instance Monitoring metrics all prevent scaling in to zero.
notes.explanation: Other Monitoring metrics allow it, provided the minimum number of instances is set to 0.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Target utilization metrics”
notes.evidence: If you autoscale based on any of the following, then your MIG cannot scale in to zero instances: Average CPU utilization HTTP load balancing serving capacity Monitoring metrics that come from each instance in the MIG However, you can use other Monitoring metrics when scaling in to zero instances, provided you set the minimum number of instances (autoscalingPolicy.minNumReplicas) to 0.

notes.front: What are two conditions under which predictive autoscaling works best?
notes.back: The application takes a long time to initialise (for example, over 2 minutes), and the load varies predictably with daily or weekly cycles.
notes.explanation: Both are about timing: the load can be foreseen, and new instances need time before they can serve.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Predictive autoscaling”
notes.evidence: Predictive autoscaling works best if your workload meets the following criteria: Your application takes a long time to initialize—for example, if you configure a initialization period of more than 2 minutes. Your workload varies predictably with daily or weekly cycles.

notes.front: How do sole-tenant nodes help with licences charged per core or per processor?
notes.back: They meet dedicated-hardware requirements and give visibility of the underlying hardware, so you can track core and processor usage.
notes.explanation: Licence terms counted per core need a way to count the cores actually used, and sole-tenancy gives that visibility.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sole-tenancy overview”, “Sole-tenancy overview”
notes.evidence: Sole-tenant nodes can help you meet dedicated hardware requirements for bring your own license (BYOL) scenarios that require per-core or per-processor licenses. When you use sole-tenant nodes, you have some visibility into the underlying hardware, which lets you track core and processor usage.

notes.front: What are two kinds of workload that might benefit from sole-tenant nodes?
notes.back: Finance or healthcare workloads with security and compliance requirements; Windows workloads with licensing requirements.
notes.explanation: The list is open: gaming workloads with performance requirements are among the others, and the source says only that they “might benefit”.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sole-tenancy overview”, “Workload considerations”
notes.evidence: The following types of workloads might benefit from using sole-tenant nodes: Gaming workloads with performance requirements Finance or healthcare workloads with security and compliance requirements Windows workloads with licensing requirements

notes.front: What are the two main components of VM Manager’s Patch feature?
notes.back: Patch compliance reporting and patch deployment.
notes.explanation: Reporting shows patch status across Windows and Linux VMs; deployment automates the patch update process.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About Patch”, “About Patch”
notes.evidence: The Patch feature has two main components: Patch compliance reporting, which provides insights on the patch status of your VM instances across Windows and Linux distributions. Along with the insights, you can also view recommendations for your VM instances. Patch deployment, which automates the operating system and software patch update process.

notes.front: Does VM Manager patch VMs that belong to a managed instance group by default?
notes.back: No. By default it patches no VMs in a MIG, although you can override this.
notes.explanation: MIG members are left alone unless you deliberately change the default.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About Patch”, “Limitations”
notes.evidence: By default, VM Manager does not patch any VMs that are part of a managed instance group (MIG). You can override this default behavior

notes.front: In GKE, what does Google Cloud manage in every cluster, and what else does it manage in Autopilot mode?
notes.back: The control plane and system components in every cluster; in Autopilot mode, the worker nodes as well.
notes.explanation: The control plane runs system components such as the Kubernetes API server.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “How GKE works”
notes.evidence: Kubernetes clusters have a set of management nodes called the control plane, which run system components such as the Kubernetes API server. In GKE, Google Cloud manages the control plane and system components for you. In Autopilot mode, which is the recommended way to run GKE, Google Cloud also manages your worker nodes.

notes.front: Which GKE mode of operation is Google’s best practice, and when should you use the other one?
notes.back: Autopilot. Use Standard mode only if you have a specific need to manage node pools and clusters manually.
notes.explanation: In Autopilot, Google Cloud manages your nodes and gives a workload-focused, cost-optimised, production-ready experience.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “Modes of operation”
notes.evidence: Best practice: Use the fully managed Autopilot mode, in which Google Cloud manages your nodes for you and provides a workload-focused, cost-optimized, production-ready experience. Only use Standard mode if you know you have a specific need to manually manage the node pools and clusters.

notes.front: GKE Autopilot clusters are always {{c1::regional}}.
notes.explanation: A regional cluster has control plane replicas across several zones of a region; a zonal cluster has a single control plane in one zone.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About cluster configuration choices”, “Availability”
notes.evidence: You can choose between regional clusters that have multiple control plane replicas across multiple compute zones in a Google Cloud region, or zonal clusters with a single control plane in a single zone. Autopilot clusters are always regional.

notes.front: Can you turn a zonal GKE cluster into a regional one after creating it?
notes.back: No. Neither can a regional cluster become zonal: the choice is fixed at creation.
notes.explanation: So the availability level must be decided before the cluster is created.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About cluster configuration choices”, “Availability”
notes.evidence: These settings can't be updated after cluster creation: a zonal cluster can't become a regional cluster, and a regional cluster can't become a zonal cluster.

notes.front: In a zonal GKE cluster, what happens when the control plane’s zone has an outage?
notes.back: Workloads keep running, but the cluster, its nodes and its workloads can’t be configured until the control plane is available again.
notes.explanation: A zonal cluster has a single control plane in a single zone, so losing that zone removes the means of configuring it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About cluster configuration choices”, “Zonal clusters”
notes.evidence: Zonal clusters have a single control plane in a single zone. Workloads still run during a cluster upgrade or an outage of the zone where the control plane runs. However, the cluster, its nodes, and its workloads can't be configured until the control plane is available.

notes.front: Which GKE setting completely isolates workloads from public networks?
notes.back: Private nodes, which you can enable for a whole cluster, a node pool (Standard) or a workload (Autopilot).
notes.explanation: A setting at node pool or workload level overrides the cluster-level node configuration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About cluster configuration choices”, “Network isolation choices”
notes.evidence: You can choose to enable private nodes in your cluster to completely isolate workloads from public networks. You can enable private nodes for entire clusters or at the node pool (for Standard) or workload (for Autopilot) level. Enabling private nodes at the node pool or workload level overrides any node configuration at the cluster level.

notes.front: What must be true for code written in any programming language to run on Cloud Run?
notes.back: You must be able to build a container image from it.
notes.explanation: Even that is optional for supported languages such as Go, Node.js, Python or Java, where source-based deployment builds the container for you.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “What is Cloud Run”
notes.evidence: You can deploy code written in any programming language on Cloud Run if you can build a container image from it. In fact, building container images is optional. If you're using Go, Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, Ruby, or a supported framework you can use the source-based deployment option that builds the container for you

notes.front: How many resource types can run your code on Cloud Run?
notes.back: Four: not just services and jobs, but also worker pools and instances.
notes.explanation: All four run sandboxed container instances in the same execution environment.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: On Cloud Run, your code can run as a service, job, worker pool, or instance. All of these resource types run sandboxed container instances in the same execution environment and can integrate with Google Cloud services.

notes.front: Which Cloud Run resource type responds to HTTP requests sent to a unique, stable endpoint?
notes.back: A service.
notes.explanation: Its container instances are stateless and support both autoscaling and manual scaling; it also responds to events and functions.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Service Responds to HTTP requests sent to a unique and stable endpoint, using stateless container instances that support both dynamic autoscaling and manual scaling, also responds to events and functions.

notes.front: Which Cloud Run resource type executes parallelisable tasks, manually or on a schedule, and runs them to completion?
notes.back: A job.
notes.explanation: Its tasks can run in parallel, and the job ends when they are complete.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Job Executes parallelizable tasks that are executed manually, or on a schedule, and run to completion.

notes.front: Which Cloud Run resource type handles always-on background workloads, such as work from message queues?
notes.back: A worker pool.
notes.explanation: The examples given are queues such as Kafka, Pub/Sub and RabbitMQ.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Worker pool Handles always-on background workloads such as workloads from message queues (Kafka, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ).

notes.front: Which Cloud Run resource type runs long-lived workloads that need a singleton runtime environment?
notes.back: An instance.
notes.explanation: A singleton runtime environment is a single one, not a scaled set of copies.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Instance Runs long-lived workloads that need a singleton runtime environment.

notes.front: What is the drawback of a Cloud Run service scaling to zero?
notes.back: The first requests after an idle spell can take longer, because Cloud Run must create a new instance.
notes.explanation: How much longer depends on how quickly the container becomes ready to handle traffic.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Scale to zero”
notes.evidence: When a new request arrives for a service with no active instances, Cloud Run creates a new instance. This process can increase the response time for these initial requests, depending on how quickly your container becomes ready to handle traffic.

notes.front: What was Cloud Run functions (1st gen) formerly called?
notes.back: Cloud Functions (1st gen).
notes.explanation: It is the original version of functions, with limited event triggers, runtimes and configurability.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compare Cloud Run functions”, “Comparison”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run functions (1st gen), formerly known as Cloud Functions (1st gen), is the original version of functions with limited event triggers, runtimes, and configurability.

notes.front: What was the latest version of Cloud Run functions formerly called?
notes.back: Cloud Functions (2nd gen).
notes.explanation: In this version, a function is a Cloud Run service deployed from source code.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compare Cloud Run functions”, “Concepts”
notes.evidence: Cloud Run functions Cloud Run functions (1st gen) Former product name Cloud Functions (2nd gen) Cloud Functions (1st gen) Resource model A function is a Cloud Run service that is deployed from source code

notes.front: What does Google recommend that new Google Cloud users choose in preference to App Engine?
notes.back: Cloud Run.
notes.explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed, modern hosting platform with advanced capabilities, such as GPUs, at lower prices.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose an App Engine environment”, “Choose an App Engine environment”
notes.evidence: Important: For new Google Cloud users, we recommend using Cloud Run as the preferred alternative over App Engine. Cloud Run is a fully managed, modern application hosting platform that provides access to advanced capabilities, such as GPUs, at lower prices.

notes.front: Why can teams keep their existing VMware tools and skills on Google Cloud VMware Engine?
notes.back: It includes the VMware stack itself, such as vSphere, vCenter and vSAN, so it is fully compatible.
notes.explanation: Compatibility covers tools, skills training and the processes of teams already familiar with VMware.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”
notes.evidence: VMware Engine includes vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX, HCX, and corresponding tools, so it's fully compatible with your existing VMware tools, skills training, and the processes used by teams already familiar with VMware.

notes.front: A team is moving an in-memory analytics database to Compute Engine. It needs far more memory for each core than typical web servers do. Which machine family fits best?
notes.back: C: Memory-optimized.
notes.choices:
A) Compute-optimized
B) Storage-optimized
C) Memory-optimized
D) Accelerator-optimized
notes.choicesExplained: A gives high performance per core, not more memory. B suits low core usage with high storage density. D is for workloads that need GPUs or TPUs.
notes.explanation: Memory-optimized machines offer more memory per core than the other families.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”, “Machine families resource and comparison guide”
notes.evidence: Memory-optimized—ideal for memory-intensive workloads, offering more memory per core than other machine families, with up to 12 TB of memory.

notes.front: A vendor charges for its software per vCPU. The workload needs fewer vCPUs than the nearest predefined machine type provides, and the team does not want to pay licence fees for idle vCPUs. What should the team use?
notes.back: C: a custom machine type with the vCPU count the workload needs.
notes.choices:
A) A larger predefined machine type, to leave headroom
B) A shared-core machine type
C) A custom machine type with the vCPU count the workload needs
D) A Spot VM of the nearest predefined type
notes.choicesExplained: A adds even more licensed vCPUs. B timeshares a physical core and suits only small, non-resource-intensive apps. D cuts the VM price but keeps the same vCPU count, so the licence cost stays.
notes.explanation: Setting the vCPU count yourself avoids licence costs for unused processing power.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”, “Create a VM with a custom machine type”
notes.evidence: Workloads that have per-CPU software license costs. Customize the number of vCPUs to avoid license costs for unused processing power or to match available software license counts.

notes.front: A studio renders animation frames in a large overnight batch. If some workers disappear, the batch just takes longer. Cost matters most. Which VMs should run the workers?
notes.back: B: Spot VMs.
notes.choices:
A) Sole-tenant nodes
B) Spot VMs
C) Shared-core machine types
D) Standard VMs in a stateful managed instance group
notes.choicesExplained: A buys dedicated hardware, which costs more and adds nothing a fault-tolerant batch needs. D pays full price to preserve per-instance state the batch does not need. C timeshares one core and suits only small, light apps.
notes.explanation: A fault-tolerant batch can withstand preemption: if some Spot VMs stop, the job slows but does not stop.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: If your workloads are fault-tolerant and can withstand possible VM preemption, Spot VMs can reduce your Compute Engine costs significantly. For example, batch processing jobs can run on Spot VMs. If some of those VMs stop during processing, the job slows but does not completely stop.

notes.front: A simulation on Spot VMs needs about 90 seconds to write a checkpoint when it is preempted. What should the team configure when creating the VMs?
notes.back: D: a preemption notice duration of 120 seconds.
notes.choices:
A) Live migration to a standard VM on preemption
B) A shutdown script, relying on the default shutdown period
C) The termination action set to delete
D) A preemption notice duration of 120 seconds
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Spot VM shutdown period is best effort and up to 30 seconds, too short for 90. C only changes what happens to the VM afterwards. A is impossible: Spot VMs can’t live migrate to become standard VMs.
notes.explanation: Google recommends 120 seconds for workloads that need longer than 30 seconds to handle preemption; this setting is in Preview.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Preemption process”
notes.evidence: 120 seconds (Preview): We recommend setting the preemption notice duration to 120 seconds for any workloads that need a dedicated duration or longer than 30 seconds to handle preemption.

notes.front: After a regional outage, a team must stand up identical web servers in another region as quickly as possible. What should it launch them from?
notes.back: D: the existing instance template, used by a managed instance group in the new region.
notes.choices:
A) An unmanaged instance group in the failed region
B) Hand-built VMs following a written checklist
C) A sole-tenant node group
D) The existing instance template, used by a managed instance group in the new region
notes.choicesExplained: A points at the region that has failed, and unmanaged groups cannot use templates. C isolates hardware but does not reproduce configuration. B gives no guarantee that the servers match.
notes.explanation: Templates are globally replicated, so the same configuration can be recreated anywhere in Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Disaster recovery building blocks”, “Instance templates”
notes.evidence: Instance templates are globally replicated, so you can recreate the instance anywhere in Google Cloud with the same configuration.

notes.front: A shop’s web front end runs on identical VMs and must keep serving if one zone fails. Which setup meets that?
notes.back: A: a regional MIG.
notes.choices:
A) A regional MIG
B) An unmanaged instance group
C) A zonal MIG with extra VMs
D) A single large VM with a custom machine type
notes.choicesExplained: C keeps every VM in one zone, so a zonal failure takes them all. B offers no multi-zone support. D is a single VM in a single zone.
notes.explanation: Regional MIGs spread load across zones, so the app keeps serving from the remaining zones.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Regional (multiple zone) coverage. Regional MIGs let you spread app load across multiple zones. This replication protects against zonal failures. If that happens, your app can continue serving traffic from instances running in the remaining available zones in the same region.

notes.front: In a MIG behind a load balancer, the application on one VM sometimes freezes while the VM keeps running. The load balancer stops sending it traffic, but the VM is never replaced. What should be added?
notes.back: D: an application-based health check for autohealing on the MIG.
notes.choices:
A) A larger machine type
B) A second load-balancing health check with tighter thresholds
C) Schedule-based autoscaling
D) An application-based health check for autohealing on the MIG
notes.choicesExplained: A does not detect or repair a frozen app. B still only redirects traffic: load-balancing health checks do not recreate instances. C adds capacity at set times but repairs nothing.
notes.explanation: An application-based health check verifies that the app responds; if it doesn’t, the MIG recreates the VM.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Application-based autohealing. You can also set up an application-based health check, which periodically verifies that your application responds as expected on each of the MIG's instances. If an application is not responding on a VM, the MIG automatically recreates that VM for you.

notes.front: A MIG autoscales on CPU utilisation with a target of 75%. During a sale, average utilisation across the group reaches 90%. What does the autoscaler do?
notes.back: A: adds VMs to bring utilisation back to or near 75%.
notes.choices:
A) Adds VMs to bring utilisation back to or near 75%
B) Nothing until utilisation reaches 100%
C) Replaces the VMs with larger machine types
D) Deletes VMs to save cost
notes.choicesExplained: B: the autoscaler acts on the gap from the target, not on saturation. C: the autoscaler changes the number of VMs, not their machine type. D is scaling in, which happens when utilisation is below target.
notes.explanation: The autoscaler keeps the group’s utilisation at or close to the target level.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, “Target utilization metrics”
notes.evidence: For example, if you scale based on CPU utilization, you can set your target utilization level at 75% and the autoscaler will maintain the CPU utilization of the specified group of instances at or close to 75%.

notes.front: A regulator requires that a bank’s VMs never share physical hardware with other organisations’ workloads. What should the bank use on Compute Engine?
notes.back: B: sole-tenant nodes that are not shared with other projects.
notes.choices:
A) A regional MIG
B) Sole-tenant nodes that are not shared with other projects
C) Custom machine types
D) Spot VMs
notes.choicesExplained: A spreads VMs across zones but still on shared hosts. C changes the VM shape, not who shares the host. D uses excess shared capacity.
notes.explanation: Keeping the host hardware unshared meets requirements for physical isolation from other workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sole-tenancy overview”, “Sole-tenancy overview”
notes.evidence: if you choose not to share the host hardware with other projects, you can meet security or compliance requirements with workloads that require physical isolation from other workloads or VMs.

notes.front: A security team wants to choose which operating system updates are approved, apply them to a project’s VMs on a recurring schedule, and see compliance status in one place. What should it use?
notes.back: D: VM Manager Patch.
notes.choices:
A) Autohealing
B) New instance templates for every update
C) Sole-tenant nodes
D) VM Manager Patch
notes.choicesExplained: A recreates failed VMs but does not patch them. B changes future VMs without reporting compliance on existing ones. C isolates hardware and does not patch anything.
notes.explanation: Patch offers patch approvals, flexible one-time or recurring schedules and a central dashboard for jobs and compliance.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About Patch”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Create patch approvals. You can select what patches to apply to your system from the full set of updates available for the specific operating system. Set up flexible scheduling. You can choose when to run patch updates (one-time and recurring schedules).

notes.front: A team wants to run its containers on Kubernetes, never manage nodes, and pay only for what its running Pods request. What should it choose?
notes.back: A: GKE in Autopilot mode.
notes.choices:
A) GKE in Autopilot mode
B) GKE in Standard mode
C) A MIG of Compute Engine VMs running containers
D) Google Cloud VMware Engine
notes.choicesExplained: B charges for all resources on nodes, whatever Pods request, and leaves node pools to you. C is not Kubernetes and leaves VMs to you. D runs the VMware platform, not managed Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: In Autopilot, Google Cloud manages the nodes and you pay only for the compute your running Pods request.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “Benefits of GKE”
notes.evidence: In Autopilot mode, pay only for the compute resources your running Pods request. In GKE Standard mode, you pay for all resources on nodes, regardless of Pod requests.

notes.front: A company is creating a GKE Standard cluster for production and wants the control plane to stay available if one zone fails. Which cluster type should it create?
notes.back: C: a regional cluster.
notes.choices:
A) A zonal cluster, converted to regional later if needed
B) A zonal cluster with extra nodes
C) A regional cluster
D) A zonal cluster with private nodes
notes.choicesExplained: A is impossible: a zonal cluster can’t become regional after creation. B adds nodes but keeps a single control plane in one zone. D improves network isolation, not availability.
notes.explanation: A regional cluster runs control plane replicas in several zones and is recommended for production.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About cluster configuration choices”, “Regional clusters”
notes.evidence: A regional cluster has multiple replicas of the control plane, running in multiple zones within your specified Google Cloud region.

notes.front: A small team has a containerised HTTP API with bursty traffic. It wants a stable endpoint and does not want to create or run any cluster. What fits best?
notes.back: C: a Cloud Run service.
notes.choices:
A) A GKE Standard cluster
B) A MIG of Compute Engine VMs
C) A Cloud Run service
D) A Cloud Run job
notes.choicesExplained: A requires creating and running a cluster and its node pools. B leaves the VMs and their scaling to the team. D runs tasks to completion; it does not serve an endpoint.
notes.explanation: A service answers HTTP requests at a unique, stable endpoint, and Cloud Run needs no cluster.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Services, jobs, worker pools, and instances”
notes.evidence: Service Responds to HTTP requests sent to a unique and stable endpoint, using stateless container instances that support both dynamic autoscaling and manual scaling

notes.front: A containerised script cleans up files once a night, then exits. On Cloud Run, which resource type should run it?
notes.back: D: a job.
notes.choices:
A) A service
B) A worker pool
C) An instance
D) A job
notes.choicesExplained: A serves requests at an endpoint. B handles always-on background work such as message queues. C runs long-lived workloads that need a singleton environment.
notes.explanation: Code that performs work and then stops is what jobs are for, and they can run on a schedule.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Cloud Run jobs”
notes.evidence: If your code performs work and then stops, for example by using a script, you can use a Cloud Run job to run your code. You can execute a job from the command line by using the Google Cloud CLI, by scheduling a recurring job, or by running it as part of a workflow.

notes.front: An internal Cloud Run service is idle most of the night, and the first morning request is slow. Users want that first response to be quick. What should the team change?
notes.back: D: set a minimum number of instances.
notes.choices:
A) Raise the request timeout
B) Lower the maximum number of instances
C) Switch to a Cloud Run job
D) Set a minimum number of instances
notes.choicesExplained: A lets slow requests run longer but does not remove the wait for a new instance. B limits scale-out and does nothing for an idle service. C runs tasks to completion and does not serve requests.
notes.explanation: Keeping a minimum of instances active stops the service from scaling to zero, so no new instance has to start for the first request.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Change scaling behavior”
notes.evidence: Minimum instances: Configure Cloud Run to keep a minimum amount of instances active so that your service doesn't scale to zero.

notes.front: A team is writing a new single-purpose function and wants Cloud Run features such as GPUs and volume mounts. Which option should it deploy to?
notes.back: B: Cloud Run functions, the latest version.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Run functions (1st gen)
B) Cloud Run functions, the latest version
C) App Engine standard environment
D) A Compute Engine VM with a custom machine type
notes.choicesExplained: A is the original version, with limited event triggers, runtimes and configurability. C is not a functions platform, and Google recommends Cloud Run for new users. D means running and patching a VM yourself.
notes.explanation: Deployed to Cloud Run, a function gets complete control, including GPUs and volume mounts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Compare Cloud Run functions”, “Configuration”
notes.evidence: When you deploy a function to Cloud Run, you have complete access and control over the function's behavior. For example, you can enable Direct VPC, configure GPUs, use volume mounts, and more.

notes.front: A company runs hundreds of workloads on VMware on-premises. It wants to move them to Google Cloud quickly without changing its VMware tools, skills or processes. What should it use?
notes.back: C: Google Cloud VMware Engine.
notes.choices:
A) Rebuild every workload as Compute Engine VMs
B) Containerise everything onto GKE
C) Google Cloud VMware Engine
D) Sole-tenant nodes running Compute Engine VMs
notes.choicesExplained: A and B both mean re-platforming and new tooling. D gives dedicated hosts but not the VMware platform.
notes.explanation: VMware Engine includes the VMware stack, so existing tools, skills and processes carry over.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”, “Google Cloud VMware Engine overview”
notes.evidence: VMware Engine includes vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX, HCX, and corresponding tools, so it's fully compatible with your existing VMware tools, skills training, and the processes used by teams already familiar with VMware.

notes.front: How do Spot VMs differ from standard VMs?
notes.back: Spot VMs cost much less but Compute Engine can preempt them at any time, so they suit fault-tolerant workloads.
notes.explanation: The price difference is the reward for accepting that the capacity can be reclaimed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Spot VMs”
notes.evidence: This provisioning model lets you obtain resources at much lower prices compared to standard VMs. However, Compute Engine can preempt Spot VMs at any time to reclaim resources. Use Spot VMs to reduce costs for fault-tolerant workloads.

notes.front: How do unmanaged instance groups differ from MIGs?
notes.back: They hold mixed VMs that you add, remove and manage yourself, without MIG features such as autoscaling, autohealing or templates.
notes.explanation: Use them if you need to load-balance groups of heterogeneous instances or to manage the instances yourself; they are not a good fit for highly available, scalable workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Instance groups”, “Unmanaged instance groups”
notes.evidence: Unmanaged instance groups can contain heterogeneous instances that you can arbitrarily add and remove from the group. Unmanaged instance groups do not offer autoscaling, autohealing, rolling update support, multi-zone support, or the use of instance templates and are not a good fit for deploying highly available and scalable workloads.

notes.front: How does billing differ between GKE Autopilot and GKE Standard?
notes.back: Autopilot: you pay for the compute your running Pods request. Standard: you pay for all resources on the nodes, whatever the Pods request.
notes.explanation: In Standard mode, node capacity that Pods don’t request is still billed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “Benefits of GKE”
notes.evidence: In Autopilot mode, pay only for the compute resources your running Pods request. In GKE Standard mode, you pay for all resources on nodes, regardless of Pod requests.

notes.front: How do Cloud Run’s request-based and instance-based billing settings differ?
notes.back: Request-based: no charge while an instance isn’t processing requests, plus a per-request fee. Instance-based: charged for the instance’s whole lifetime, with no per-request fee.
notes.explanation: The two settings trade a per-request fee against paying for idle time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Cloud Run”, “Pay-per-use pricing for services”
notes.evidence: Request-based If an instance is not processing requests, you're not charged. You pay a per-request fee. Instance-based You're charged for the entire lifetime of an instance. There's no per-request fee.

notes.front: How do the App Engine standard and flexible environments differ in start-up time and scaling to zero?
notes.back: Standard starts instances in seconds and can scale to zero; flexible starts in minutes and keeps at least one instance.
notes.explanation: In the comparison table, faster start-up and scaling to zero are on the standard side; flexible offers background processes and a modifiable runtime instead.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose an App Engine environment”, “Compare high-level features”
notes.evidence: Instance startup time Seconds Minutes Maximum request timeout Depends on the runtime and type of scaling. 60 minutes Background threads Yes, with restrictions Yes Background processes No Yes SSH debugging No Yes Scaling Manual, Basic, Automatic Manual, Automatic Scale to zero Yes No, minimum 1 instance

notes.front: When is GKE a better fit than a fully managed platform such as Cloud Run?
notes.back: When you need to configure the infrastructure that runs your containers, such as networking, scaling, hardware and security.
notes.explanation: GKE still manages many underlying components, such as the control plane and nodes, while giving you Kubernetes’ operational power.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “GKE overview”, “When to use GKE”
notes.evidence: GKE is ideal if you need a platform that lets you configure the infrastructure that runs your containerized apps, such as networking, scaling, hardware, and security. GKE provides the operational power of Kubernetes while managing many of the underlying components, such as the control plane and nodes, for you.
